entries.title: Who Writes the Law — an atlas of corporate capture of lawmaking
Cross-border studies
entries.kind: 24 findings that cover many countries at once
entries.html:
Which laws the evidence concerns, worldwide

Documented cases include the cross-border findings below. Sector indices count countries in the worst quarter on that area's index; for elections, countries whose law bans neither corporate nor contractor donations.

Area of lawDocumented casesSector indices
Foreign and security policy5 · 3 countries—
Tax and financial secrecy2 · 2 countries141 countries
Banking and finance9 · 8 countries—
Environment, energy and resources11 · 8 countries18 countries
Health and tobacco42 · 37 countries100 countries
Elections and political money6 · 4 countries178 countries
Public contracts and spending28 · 18 countries—
Labour and social protection6 · 2 countries—
Technology and data3 · 1 country—
Other business regulation15 · 10 countries—
Policy in general82 · 41 countries—
Policy follows the affluent

Legislators match the affluent around the world

52 countries

Matching every available survey of elected legislators to mass surveys — 92,000 legislator and 3.9 million citizen responses across 52 countries and 33 years — researchers found legislators' views are consistently closer to those of affluent citizens on economic issues. On cultural issues, the poor appeared over-represented.

  • Lupu & Warner, 'Affluence and Congruence: Unequal Representation around the World', Journal of Politics (2022)Academic, peer-reviewed · archived copy
Lobbying money

Governments that don't know who lobbies them

< half of OECD

Less than half of OECD countries know who is lobbying their governments, because the work is often done indirectly or through proxies. Only Australia, Canada and the U.S. had rules on lobbying by foreign governments.

  • OECD, 'Lobbying in the 21st Century' press release (2021)Intergovernmental (OECD) · archived copy
Lobbying money

Big Tech in Brussels

€151 million/yr

The tech industry spends about €151 million a year lobbying EU institutions (up over 50% in four years); Meta alone declares €10 million. Its 890 full-time lobbyists outnumber the 720 members of the European Parliament. Business overall was set to spend at least €381.7 million in 2026.

  • Euronews on Corporate Europe Observatory & LobbyControl study (Oct 2025)Journalism relaying advocacy-group analysis of EU register · archived copy
  • EU Perspectives on CEO & LobbyControl study (2025)Journalism relaying advocacy-group analysis · archived copy
  • Malay Mail (AFP) on CEO & LobbyControl June 2026 reportJournalism relaying advocacy-group analysis · archived copy
Law written or shaped by industry

EU reuses tech companies' arguments

AFP reported in 2026 that an Investigate Europe investigation found the EU had reused tech companies' arguments almost word for word to avoid requiring detailed disclosure of data centers' environmental footprint. The original investigation was not checked for this map.

  • AFP report (via Fortuneo) citing an Investigate Europe investigationJournalism, secondhand — original not checked · archived copy
Policy follows the affluent

Social spending ignores the poor in 30 democracies

30 countries

Using 160 surveys from 1985 to 2012 in 30 countries, Larry Bartels found social-spending decisions responded powerfully to the preferences of affluent citizens but not at all, or even negatively, to those of poor citizens.

  • Bartels, 'Political Inequality in Affluent Democracies: The Social Welfare Deficit' (2017)Academic working paper · archived copy
Law written or shaped by industry

Lobby papers copied into EU privacy-law amendments

dozens of amendments

Comparing lobby papers with amendments to the EU's draft Data Protection Regulation, campaigner Max Schrems found dozens of amendments copied word for word from papers by Amazon, eBay, the American Chamber of Commerce and the European Banking Federation; three British MEPs' amendments were over 22% copied text.

  • Privacy International, on the LobbyPlag findings (2013)Advocacy group · archived copy
Law written or shaped by industry

Industry-written amendments to EU hedge fund rules

1,600 amendments

About 1,600 amendments were tabled to the EU directive regulating hedge funds and private equity; according to sources in the Parliament cited by Corporate Europe Observatory, more than half were written by industry lobbies and passed on by sympathetic MEPs.

  • Corporate Europe Observatory, 'MEP amendments and democracy'Advocacy watchdog, citing unnamed parliamentary sources · archived copy
Policy follows the affluent

Latin Americans say they are governed for the powerful

72%

Across 17 Latin American countries surveyed by Latinobarómetro in 2023, 72% said their country is governed by a few powerful groups for their own benefit; 24% said it is governed for the good of all.

  • El Financiero on Latinobarómetro 2023Latinobarómetro survey, as reported by a news outlet · archived copy
Lobbying money

Politicians who own or run big companies

7.76% of world market value

In a study of nearly 20,000 listed firms in 42 countries, firms whose controlling shareholders or top officers sat in parliament or government made up 2.68% of listed firms but 7.76% of world stock-market value. They enjoyed easier credit, lower taxes and larger market shares, especially in countries with more corruption.

  • Faccio, 'Politically connected firms: Can they squeeze the state?' (working paper, 2002; published as 'Politically Connected Firms', American Economic Review, 2006)Academic · archived copy
Lobbying money

Big business fills the EU's advisory groups

52% of seats

Across the European Commission's expert groups created between September 2012 and September 2013, which advise on new EU laws, big business held 52% of seats, against 3% for small businesses and 3% for trade unions. In the tax and customs department, nearly 80% of members represented corporate interests.

  • ALTER-EU, AK EUROPA and ÖGB Europabüro, 'A Year of Broken Promises' (6 Nov 2013)Lobbying-transparency coalition · archived copy
  • Computerworld, on the ALTER-EU expert group study (2013)Journalism · archived copy
Policy follows the affluent

Across 30 European countries, the rich have an edge

about 3,000 proposals

Matching about 3,000 policy proposals from 30 European countries over nearly 40 years with whether each was implemented, researchers found policies favored by high-income citizens were more likely to be adopted, but the gap was smaller than in U.S. studies. They found no consistent link between this gap and inequality, campaign finance rules, union strength or turnout. They also note studies pointing to the same pattern in EU institutions.

  • Persson & Sundell, 'The Rich Have a Slight Edge', British Journal of Political Science (2023)Academic · archived copy
Policy follows the affluent

Latin American legislators side with the better-off

A Vanderbilt dissertation comparing legislator surveys with citizen surveys across Latin America found that in most countries, legislators' policy preferences are closer to those of better-off citizens than to the poor, and that electoral rules make little difference.

  • Corral González, 'Uneven Representation? Analysis of Democratic Responsiveness in Latin America' (PhD dissertation, Vanderbilt University, 2013)Academic (dissertation) · archived copy
Policy follows the affluent

EU institutions sit closer to the wealthy

Comparing the positions of the EU Council and European Parliament with those of citizens in different income groups, researchers found both institutions, especially the Council, sit to the right of European citizens and closer to the wealthy. The poor are systematically underrepresented in the Council, though the rich are not systematically over-represented.

  • Lefkofridi & Giger, 'Democracy or Oligarchy? Unequal Representation of Income Groups in European Institutions', Politics and Governance 8(1), 2020Academic · archived copy
Influence by a foreign government

Foreign governments buying influence in the European Parliament

€1.5 million in cash seized

In the 2022 'Qatargate' case, Belgian prosecutors allege Qatar and Morocco paid to influence the European Parliament; about €1.5 million in cash was seized. Former MEP Pier Antonio Panzeri, the alleged ringleader, agreed a plea deal admitting bribery in return for a reduced sentence and information. Others charged, including former Parliament vice-president Eva Kaili, deny wrongdoing; both governments deny the accusations.

  • ANSA, 'Qatargate: Panzeri to tell whole truth, lawyer tells ANSA' (18 Jan 2023)Journalism · archived copy
  • Brussels Times, 'Panzeri to collaborate with Belgian authorities'Journalism · archived copy
Influence by a foreign government

An MEP's reported reports to Russia's security service

In 2024 leaked emails published by The Insider and Re:Baltica showed Latvian MEP Tatjana Ždanoka corresponding since at least 2004 with officers identified as Russia's FSB, reporting on her activities including European Parliament hearings and asking for money for events. The Parliament found she breached its code of conduct on declaring interests and gifts and fined her; Latvia's security service opened a criminal case. She denies working with Russian intelligence.

  • LSM (Latvian Public Broadcasting), 'MEP Ždanoka gets penalty from European Parliament' (11 Apr 2024)Public broadcaster · archived copy
  • Novaya Gazeta Europe, 'European Parliament launches probe into Latvian MEP's alleged Russia ties' (30 Jan 2024)Journalism · archived copy
Policy follows the affluent

Most people in 107 countries say a few big interests run their government

54%

In Transparency International's 2012–13 survey of more than 114,000 people in 107 countries, 54% said their government is run largely or entirely by a few big interests acting for themselves (36% 'large extent', 19% 'entirely'), and 6% said not at all. The report publishes country figures only for its 28 OECD countries; the rest are in respondent data available from Transparency International on request.

  • Transparency International, Global Corruption Barometer 2013 (survey Sept 2012–Mar 2013; Appendix C, Table 2 and Figure 6)Public opinion survey, about 1,000 people per country in 107 countries · archived copy
Law written or shaped by industry

Twelve chief executives behind the WTO's patent rules

12 CEOs

A 12-member, US-based Intellectual Property Committee of chief executives from pharmaceutical, entertainment and software companies built international support for stronger global patent and copyright protection. With its European and Japanese business counterparts it drafted a proposal based on industrialized countries' existing laws and presented it to the GATT Secretariat in 1988. The resulting 1994 TRIPS Agreement binds every WTO member, and political scientist Susan Sell finds it closely mirrors what those executives asked for. In 1986 the members were Bristol-Myers, CBS, Du Pont, General Electric, General Motors, Hewlett-Packard, IBM, Johnson & Johnson, Merck, Monsanto and Pfizer.

  • Susan K. Sell, Private Power, Public Law: The Globalization of Intellectual Property Rights (Cambridge University Press, 2003), ch. 1 (publisher's sample)Academic book · archived copy
Law written or shaped by industry

A database of tailor-made laws in the Western Balkans and Turkey

29 laws

Transparency International documented 29 laws or regulations written to benefit particular companies, officials or networks: 9 in Serbia, 7 in Turkey, 6 in Albania, 4 in Bosnia and Herzegovina and 3 in North Macedonia. Most are classified as capturing a market, an industry or public resources; others replaced public officials or weakened checks and balances. Each appears in its country's record on this map. The project's accompanying report found Albania had the most such laws in the region.

  • Transparency International, Tailor-made laws in the Western Balkans and Turkey (database)Anti-corruption NGO database · archived copy
  • Exit News on Transparency International, 'Examining State Capture: Undue Influence on Law-Making and the Judiciary in the Western Balkans and Turkey'News report on NGO study · archived copy
Policy follows the affluent

A review of 25 studies: the rich usually come out ahead, but results vary widely

A systematic review pooled 1,163 estimates from 25 published studies of whose preferences governments follow. Comparing the rich with the poor, the rich were better represented in about two of three comparisons, the poor in 12%, the two roughly equally in 5%, and 18% were unclear. The most common single result (32%) was policy following the rich while moving against the poor, but 96% of the models producing that result put several income groups into one statistical model, a method the authors say can exaggerate gaps when groups want similar things. Studies outside the United States found larger gaps than US studies.

  • Elkjær & Klitgaard, 'Economic Inequality and Political Responsiveness: A Systematic Review', Perspectives on Politics 22(2) (2024; online 2021)Peer-reviewed systematic review (open access) · archived copy
Policy follows the affluent

Welfare generosity follows richer citizens

Linking survey answers on health, pension and unemployment policy across many democracies to later changes in how generous those programs became, researchers found that policy moved with public opinion, but far more strongly with the views of richer than poorer citizens.

  • Schakel, Burgoon & Hakhverdian, 'Real but Unequal Representation in Welfare State Reform', Politics & Society 48(1) (2020)Peer-reviewed study (open access) · archived copy
  • Elkjær & Klitgaard, 'Economic Inequality and Political Responsiveness: A Systematic Review', Perspectives on Politics 22(2) (2024; online 2021)Peer-reviewed systematic review (open access) · archived copy
Policy follows the affluent

Social spending in Europe leans toward the rich

Studying affluent, mainly European democracies, Peters and Ensink found the rich had an outsized influence on social spending, to the point that spending often moved against the preferences of the poor. They linked larger gaps to lower turnout, though the gap only became significant at turnout below 40%, lower than any country in their sample, as summarized in the 2024 systematic review.

  • Peters & Ensink (2015), as summarized in Elkjær & Klitgaard (2024)Peer-reviewed study, via systematic review · archived copy
Policy follows the affluent

A dissenting finding: the middle class sets long-run spending

Using preferences on redistribution and social spending in 21 democracies, Elkjær and Iversen found that short-term changes in spending tracked the preferences of the rich, but long-run spending levels tracked the middle class. They argue that because richer people are better informed, standard methods can make the rich look decisive even when the middle class is.

  • Elkjær & Iversen (2020), as summarized in Elkjær & Klitgaard (2024)Peer-reviewed study, via systematic review · archived copy
Law written or shaped by industry

A tobacco industry template copied into smoking laws across two continents

In the late 1990s Philip Morris paid for 'accommodation' programmes, run through the International Hotels & Restaurants Association, to offer bars and restaurants an alternative to smoking bans; by 1999 they covered 8,357 venues in 47 countries at a cost of about US$15 million. Spain's 2005 tobacco law (in force 2006) wrote both programme concepts into law: separate smoking areas in venues over 100 m² and owner's choice in smaller ones. Researchers found that by 2011 at least nine European and five Latin American countries had adopted similar size-based exceptions nationally or in provinces, and that all of them except the German-speaking countries and Croatia had earlier hosted Philip Morris's programmes. Spain itself removed the exceptions in 2011.

  • Schneider, Sebrié & Fernández, 'The so-called "Spanish model" – Tobacco industry strategies and its impact in Europe and Latin America', BMC Public Health 11:907 (2011)Peer-reviewed study of internal industry documents (open access) · archived copy
Law written or shaped by industry

EU tobacco directive moved toward industry submissions

Scoring the wording of submissions from 18 stakeholders on a scale from the tobacco industry's position to public-health groups' position, researchers tracked the EU Tobacco Products Directive from the European Commission's 2010 consultation through its 2012 proposal to the law approved in March 2014. They found the text shifted significantly toward the tobacco industry's submissions as industry lobbying went on; retailers, trade unions and publishers took positions closer to the industry than to health groups.

  • Costa, Gilmore, Peeters, McKee & Stuckler, 'Quantifying the influence of the tobacco industry on EU governance: automated content analysis of the EU Tobacco Products Directive', Tobacco Control 23(6) (2014)Peer-reviewed study (open access) · archived copy
  • University of Oxford news release on the study (2014)University news release · archived copy

entries.title: How it's ranked
entries.html:
Each of thirty-one published measures is converted into a position from 0 to 100 among the countries it covers, where 100 means the most captured. A country's score is the weighted average of the positions it has, plus a pull toward 50 equal to two full-weight measures, so a country with thin data cannot land at either extreme: a country with most of the measures barely moves, while one with a single measure is pulled noticeably toward the middle. The last slider under "How the score is built" changes that pull. The score is this map's own combination, not a finding of any one study. Seven of the thirty-one measures are expert ratings from V-Dem and two come from the World Justice Project's surveys, so those two projects shape much of the result. Documented cases and named people are shown on the map but do not enter the score, because they mostly reflect where journalists and courts have looked. The documented cases and named people are a small and uneven sample of what happens, not a count of it. No study has measured how many laws are captured in any country, so no reliable percentage can be given; the map's own sources show the scale instead. One U.S. investigation found more than 10,000 bills copied almost word for word from model legislation in eight years, over 2,100 of which became law, and file data from Brazil's Congress revealed 2,176 proposals written by lobbyists since 2019; each appears on this map as a single case. Most influence is legal and unrecorded where there are no lobby registers or disclosure rules. Everything shown is real, sourced data, but it reflects where journalists, courts and researchers have looked. Lawsuits that foreign investors bring against governments are left out entirely: they challenge laws after they are made and say nothing about who shaped them.

Weights follow how directly a measure observes lawmakers and lawmaking, and how independent, recent and widely covering it is. The top 1% income share from the World Inequality Database is included at weight 0: it shows how concentrated the money is that could buy influence, but it does not measure influence itself, so it changes the score only if you raise its slider. Full weight (1) goes to expert and survey ratings of the wealthy's hold on power, legislators trading favors, legislators using office for private gain, and whether the legislature can check the executive. Three-quarter weight goes to budgets aimed at narrow interests and regulation bent by improper influence, which sit one step from lawmaking, and to tobacco interference, which covers one industry. Half weight goes to whether courts can check the executive, the military's hold on government and clientelism (each a route by which lawmaking is taken from the public, but one step removed from the legislature), to the Global Data Barometer's score for published lobbying, political-finance and asset data (it measures openness about influence rather than influence), to measures of law design or single sectors (financial secrecy, corporate tax havens, bans on corporate and contractor donations, resource governance), to Europe's 2015 lobbying review, to Bertelsmann's anti-corruption scores (BTI for developing and transition countries, SGI for 30 OECD and EU countries), to the OECD's check of lobbying, conflict-of-interest and political-finance safeguards (which measures safeguards rather than influence), to the public's 2012–13 ratings of how corrupt parliament is (direct about the legislature, but about corruption generally and over a decade old), to criminal groups operating inside government (which covers all illegal markets, not only lawmaking), to the World Bank's 2017–18 record of whether draft regulations are opened to public comment and the Africa Integrity Indicators' 2025 ratings of access to lawmaking, asset disclosure and party-donation disclosure (both measure openness rather than influence; the African ratings also feed the World Bank's corruption measure), and to the World Bank's corruption measure, which partly re-uses V-Dem and World Justice Project data and would otherwise double-count them. Quarter weight goes to the 1999, 2002 and 2005 bought-laws surveys and the 2001 study of politicians' firms because of their age. Every weight can be changed with the sliders.
